::: {.why}
The plateau you found last night is what happens when you repeat a drill without changing it, and breaking a plateau requires a different exercise rather than more repetitions.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Identify which specific arithmetic operations are slowest and drill those rather than the whole set.
- Improve the timed score on your slowest operation by a measurable amount.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Diagnose rather than repeat: time each operation type separately, which is two-digit multiplication, percentage of a number, fraction to decimal, division, and compounding. One of them is far slower than the others and that is where the whole time goes.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Drill the slow one with a technique rather than by repetition: complements for multiplication near a round number, the difference of squares for numbers straddling a multiple of ten, and the reciprocal table for fractions. Learn the specific technique, then retest and report the improvement.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Rebuild the daily drill around what you found, so the remaining sittings train the weak operation rather than the whole set.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Jane Street — puzzles](https://www.janestreet.com/puzzles/) [problems]{.res-kind}
- [Grinstead & Snell — Introduction to Probability (free PDF)](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf) [textbook]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Per-operation timings with the slowest identified, a technique learned for it, and the measured improvement.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Which arithmetic operation is your slowest, and what technique did you learn for it?
:::
